---
title: Overview
---

This project provides a structured examination of the data science lifecycle, focusing on the core stages of data collection, cleaning, exploratory data analysis (EDA), and modeling through both supervised and unsupervised methods. Above all, this project is about the math. Rather than treating statistical and machine learning methods as black boxes, each one is presented alongside the mathematics that underlies it, including definitions, derivations, and the reasoning that connects a formula to the code that implements it. The emphasis is therefore placed less on final model performance or conclusions and more on the processes, assumptions, and methodological decisions that shape each stage, and on understanding why each method works the way it does.

Data collection is conducted using the Python library `pybaseball`, which serves as a wrapper for multiple baseball data sources, including FanGraphs and Statcast. This approach highlights how modern data science workflows often rely on APIs and abstraction layers to gather large, heterogeneous datasets from multiple providers efficiently.

The data cleaning phase centers on constructing a unified and analysis-ready dataset in the form of a pandas `DataFrame`, ultimately exported as a CSV file. Each row corresponds to a single Statcast-qualified MLB hitter season from 2017 through 2024, excluding the shortened 2020 season. A hitter season is Statcast-qualified if it has at least 200 plate appearances and meets Baseball Savant's minimum number of batted-ball events for that season. Only Statcast-qualified seasons with no missing values are kept. Aside from a few identifying columns (season, player name, and team), each column represents a relevant performance metric. These features span traditional counting statistics (e.g., home runs), advanced sabermetrics (e.g., weighted runs created), and Statcast-derived measures (e.g., average home run distance). The cleaning process also involves aligning data across sources via player ID crosswalks, removing incomplete records, and ensuring consistency in labels and units.

The EDA is meant to identify patterns, relationships, and potential anomalies within the dataset. Visualization tools such as `matplotlib`, `seaborn`, and `plotly` are employed to generate a variety of plots, including correlation heatmaps and distributions. This stage emphasizes interpretability and intuition-building, illustrating how different statistical measures relate to one another and how the underlying structure of the data can inform subsequent modeling choices. The plots are grounded in the statistics behind them, such as the Pearson correlation coefficient, the normal distribution, and standardization with $Z$-scores.

The modeling component introduces several foundational machine learning techniques. On the supervised side, these include simple and multiple linear regression, which examine relationships between statistics, and multiple logistic regression, which predicts binary outcomes. On the unsupervised side, both methods are applied to the 2024 season: $K$-means clustering is used to uncover latent groupings among hitters, and principal component analysis (PCA) is used to reduce the dimensionality of the data for visualization. Rather than optimizing model performance, the focus is on the mathematics of each algorithm: the loss functions it minimizes, how its parameters are estimated (whether in closed form, as with ordinary least squares, or iteratively, as with gradient descent), the linear algebra behind methods such as PCA, and the assumptions each one makes. Applying these methods to baseball statistics then shows how that theory plays out on real data.
